newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hails job rise, seeks help on welfare.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails job rise, seeks help on welfare.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Friday hailed a strong rise in U.S. job growth and exhorted businessmen to help move people from welfare to work, saying welfare reform "cannot succeed by government action alone."

Speaking after the Labour Department reported the economy generated 262,000 new jobs last month, Clinton said the rise was "good news," adding that neither he, nor Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, saw signs of inflationary pressures.

The report, which also revised up the October and November job creation figures, showed that the unemployment rate held steady at 5.3 percent and that 11.2 million jobs have been generated during Clinton's first four years in office.

"This is the first time in the history of our economy that over 11 million jobs have been created during one four-year administration," Clinton told reporters at the start of a White House event on moving people from welfare to work.

"It is a great tribute to the private sector of America and further evidence that our economy is strong and, finally, that our economic strategy to bring down the deficit, expand trade and invest in our people is working," Clinton added.

Asked if he was concerned that the figures may presage a build up in inflationary pressures, Clinton said he was not, adding that Greenspan had told him in a meeting on Wednesday that he also does not see these in the economy.

"One of the things that he (Greenspan) noted ... was that the normal inflation pressures, at least if you go back till the end of World War Two, that you would see with this kind of job growth and, by modern standards, a low unemployment rate, just have not materialised," Clinton said.
"I basically believe as long as we're competitive ... that we can keep this going without undue inflation," he added. "At least now there is no evidence of it (inflation)."

Clinton invited more than a dozen businessmen, including the chief executives of Burger King, a unit of Britain's Grand Metropolitan Plc, Sprint Corp and UAL Corp, the parent of United Airlines, to the White House to highlight his efforts to move people from welfare to work.

In August the president signed a welfare reform law ending the 61-year federal guarantee of aid to the poor, giving states broad power to design their own programmes, and limiting such public assistance to five years.
As he has often done since signing the law, much reviled by many liberals, Clinton bluntly said it would not work without a greater effort by companies to hire such people.

"Welfare reform, if it is going to work, will have to have the leadership of the private sector in turning welfare checks into pay checks," Clinton said. "Unless we can create new jobs in the private sector within the two-year time frame, the welfare reform effort will not succeed."

The law limits most benefits to five years and requires recipients to work after two years. States can set up individual plans setting out job goals for welfare recipients and can reduce aid to families if a recipient does not comply.

Clinton also told the businessmen his new budget would propose incentives "attractive to the private sector" to encourage the hiring of welfare recipients. In part, he was referring to tax incentives unveiled during the 1996 campaign.
Despite Clinton's meeting with the executives, some in industry said they need more help to hire people off welfare.

"American business will find it difficult moving people from welfare to work without an expanded commitment from Congress and the ... administration to pass other common-sense training, preparation and community work force programmes," said the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, a leading business lobby.
